Performance What is retained

Each benchmark job uploads its latest number as badge JSON. Those snapshots accumulate in a history file on gh-pages so the performance page shows trends rather than only the latest reading.

Publishing How it fits together

The Pages publisher fetches each benchmark's latest artifact by name, so a benchmark that failed today keeps its last good number on the site.

docs.title: Tracked benchmarks
docs.text:
All five are measured by qemu-minimal-report-for-vm-rocm-golden.yml against one stack, described by qemu/stacks/rocm-golden.xml: two guests from the published rocm-golden image, each with a GPU, an NVMe, an RDMA NIC and an SDXI device. The lane runs that file unmodified, so the numbers come from the QEMU it pins: the sbates-fork build since 2026-11-18, and the stock build of the same QEMU release before that, which is a step to expect in the trend lines. The two hipFile metrics step much further on the same date, by about seventy times: that file now points the guest's NVMe at its GPU's memory (<vm-nvme-vram>), so hipFile's direct read maps that memory where, most likely, it went through QEMU a page at a time before (inferred, not profiled). That is the setting and not faster code. The fio metric is fio 3.43, the first release with the libhipfile engine, from the first daily run after that change reached main. It is still built in the guest before the run, because no published golden image carries it yet; an image baked after the change has it under /opt/fio-hipfile and the build is skipped. The performance page lists such changes, with their dates, under "Changes to what is measured".

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The site is built from docs/ using MkDocs Material and pushed as pre-built HTML to the gh-pages branch.
  • No guest inspection report is published. The benchmark jobs upload badge JSON only.
  • Performance history is stored only on gh-pages; it is not committed on main.

docs.title: Site assembly
docs.text:
The published site is built from two sources:

  1. Repository-owned Pages content under docs/.
  2. The latest unexpired perf-* artifacts uploaded by the benchmark jobs.

The qemu-minimal-publish-pages.yml workflow fetches each artifact by name into a scratch directory, regenerates docs/perf/ from it, runs mkdocs build to produce site/, and pushes the built HTML to the gh-pages branch. The artifacts themselves are inputs only and are never published.

docs.title: Performance tracking flow
docs.text: Each artifact holds the badge JSON for one benchmark. The publisher reads those badges, appends a new record when metrics change, and regenerates the performance page and badge JSON from a history file on gh-pages. That keeps main free of CI-written history while retaining trends over time.

docs.title: Adding another benchmark
docs.text:
1. Have the job upload its badge-*.json under its own stable perf-<name> artifact name.
  2. Fetch that artifact in qemu-minimal-publish-pages.yml.
  3. If the job lives in a new workflow, add its name: to the workflow_run trigger list — omit this and the number publishes only when another workflow finishes.
  4. Add the metric to METRICS in scripts/render-site-perf.py.
  5. Add the endpoint badge to the README.

docs.title: Failure model
docs.text:
• A missing or expired artifact leaves that metric's last recorded value in the history; its badge reads n/a until a new number arrives.
  • Retried Pages publishes rebuild from the latest gh-pages tip before pushing.
  • Performance history is regenerated from the seeded gh-pages record, so a re-run does not truncate the trend page to one point.

docs.title: Performance trends
docs.text: This page is generated during the Pages publish from retained benchmark history on gh-pages, using the badge JSON the benchmark jobs upload as inputs. It mirrors the same basic model used by the ROCm/rocm-ernic site: badges for the latest published numbers, a durable history file, and a trend page regenerated as new CI data lands.

docs.title: Latest published snapshot
docs.text:
Generated from fddac6f2 at 2026-11-20 16:52 UTC.

Badge colour is health, not branding. Each latest reading is compared against the mean of the previous 5 distinct readings — consecutive republishes of an unchanged number are collapsed first, because a publish re-records every artifact it finds, including ones no job refreshed. Green is at or above 95% of that baseline, amber down to 80%, red below it, and blue means there is not yet a second distinct reading to compare against. The band is wide on purpose: these benchmarks run against an emulated GPU over vfio-user and swing hard between runs.

docs.title: Changes to what is measured
docs.text:
A step in a chart on or after one of these dates, at the first daily run after the change reached main, is the change named here.

Date Metrics Change 2026-11-18 HipFile Fio fio is built from the 3.43 release, the first with the libhipfile engine, where it was a master commit between 3.42 and 3.43. It is still built in the guest before the run: no published golden image carries it yet. One baked after this change has it under /opt/fio-hipfile, and the build is then skipped. 2026-11-18 Rocjitsu HipFile, HipFile Fio The stack's NVMe is pointed at the guest's GPU BAR (<vm-nvme-vram>), so hipFile's direct path maps GPU memory, where it most likely went through QEMU's 4 KiB bounce buffer before (inferred, not profiled). Measured by hand before the change: 11 to 13 MB/s without; 831 and 959 MB/s with, one run each. 2026-11-18 all Every stack and workflow moved from stock QEMU to the fork QEMU and the ernic server built against its libvfio-user.
